terms.grammar: adjective: the participle of commoveō, often with the ablative of the cause
evidence: Cic. Fam. 3.10.1: graviter prīmō nūntiō commōtus sum
terms.comment: Latin says what moved the person and how much: graviter, vehementer commōtus. Without context it leans to agitation or distress (see affect).

evidence: Cic. Att. 10.4.6 (Lewis & Short): sīve īrācundiā, sīve dolōre, sīve metū permōtus
terms.comment: Stronger than commōtus: thoroughly stirred, by anger, grief or fear; also “persuaded, induced” (Lewis & Short, s.v. permoveō).

terms.gloss: be unable to hold back one’s tears
terms.comment: Where English says “I got emotional”, Latin usually names the tears: sine lacrimīs, lacrimās tenēre.

phrases.latin: ad tē vērō et ad nostram Tulliolam nōn queō sine plūrimīs lacrimīs scrībere
phrases.english: but to you and our little Tullia I can’t write without many tears

phrases.latin: haec tibi rīdicula videntur; nōn enim ades. quae sī vidērēs, lacrimās nōn tenērēs.
phrases.english: these things seem funny to you, for you aren’t here. If you saw them, you couldn’t hold back your tears.

sources: Lewis & Short: commotus · Lewis & Short: permoveo · Lewis & Short: lacrima
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 159.
